{{Short description|Graph representing a permutation}}
[[Image:Permutation graph.svg|thumb|300px|The permutation graph and the [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] diagram for the permutation {{math|(4,3,5,1,2)}}]]

In the [[mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], a '''permutation graph''' is a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] whose [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] represent the elements of a [[permutation]], and whose edges represent pairs of elements that are [[Inversion (discrete mathematics)|reversed]] by the permutation. Permutation graphs may also be defined [[Geometric graph theory|geometrically]], as the [[intersection graph]]s of line segments whose endpoints lie on two [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] lines. Different permutations may give rise to the same permutation graph; a given graph has a unique representation (up to permutation [[symmetry]]) if it is [[Prime graph|prime]] with respect to the [[modular decomposition]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Le|Spinrad|1999}}, p.191.</ref>

==Definition and characterization==
If <math>\rho = (\sigma_1,\sigma_2,...,\sigma_n)</math> is any [[permutation]] of the numbers from <math>1</math> to <math>n</math>, then one may define a permutation graph from <math>\sigma</math> in which there are <math>n</math> [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] <math>v_1, v_2, ..., v_n</math>, and in which there is an edge <math>v_i v_j</math> for any two indices <math>i < j</math> for which <math>j</math> appears before <math>i</math> in <math>\rho</math>. That is, two indices <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> determine an edge in the permutation graph exactly when they determine an [[Inversion (discrete mathematics)|inversion]] in the permutation.

Given a permutation <math>\sigma</math>, one may also determine a set of [[line segment]]s <math>s_i</math> with endpoints <math>(i,0)</math> and <math>(k, 1)</math>, such that <math>\sigma_k=i</math>. The endpoints of these segments lie on the two parallel lines <math>y=0</math> and <math>y=1</math>, and two segments have a non-empty intersection if and only if they correspond to an inversion in the permutation. Thus, the permutation graph of <math>\sigma</math> coincides with the [[intersection graph]] of the segments. For every two parallel lines, and every finite set of line segments with endpoints on both lines, the intersection graph of the segments is a permutation graph; in the case that the segment endpoints are all distinct, a permutation for which it is the permutation graph may be given by numbering the segments on one of the two lines in consecutive order, and reading off these numbers in the order that the segment endpoints appear on the other line.

Permutation graphs have several other equivalent characterizations:
* A graph <math>G</math> is a permutation graph if and only if <math>G</math> is a [[circle graph]] that admits an ''equator'', i.e., an additional [[Chord (geometry)|chord]] that intersects every other chord.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Le|Spinrad|1999}}, Proposition&nbsp;4.7.1, p.57.</ref>
*A graph <math>G</math> is a permutation graph if and only if both <math>G</math> and its [[complement graph|complement]] <math>\overline{G}</math> are [[comparability graph]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Dushnik|Miller|1941}}.</ref>
*A graph <math>G</math> is a permutation graph if and only if it is the [[comparability graph]] of a [[partially ordered set]] that has [[order dimension]] at most two.<ref>{{harvtxt|Baker|Fishburn|Roberts|1971}}.</ref>
*If a graph <math>G</math> is a permutation graph, so is its complement. A permutation that represents the complement of <math>G</math> may be obtained by reversing the permutation representing <math>G</math>.

==Efficient algorithms==
It is possible to test whether a given graph is a permutation graph, and if so construct a permutation representing it, in [[linear time]].<ref>{{harvtxt|McConnell|Spinrad|1999}}.</ref>

As a subclass of the [[perfect graph]]s, many problems that are [[NP-complete]] for arbitrary graphs may be solved efficiently for permutation graphs. For instance:

* the largest [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] in a permutation graph corresponds to the [[longest increasing subsequence|longest decreasing subsequence]] in the permutation defining the graph, so the [[clique problem]] may be solved in [[polynomial time]] for permutation graphs by using a longest decreasing subsequence algorithm.<ref>{{harvtxt|Golumbic|1980}}.</ref>
* likewise, an increasing subsequence in a permutation corresponds to an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] of the same size in the corresponding permutation graph.
* the [[treewidth]] and [[pathwidth]] of permutation graphs can be computed in polynomial time; these algorithms exploit the fact that the number of [[Vertex separator#Minimal separators|inclusion minimal vertex separators]] in a permutation graph is polynomial in the size of the graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Bodlaender|Kloks|Kratsch|1995}}</ref>

==Relation to other graph classes==
Permutation graphs are a special case of [[circle graph]]s, [[comparability graph]]s, the complements of comparability graphs, and [[trapezoid graph]]s.

The subclasses of the permutation graphs include the [[bipartite graph|bipartite]] permutation graphs (characterized by {{harvnb|Spinrad|Brandstädt|Stewart|1987}}) and the [[cograph]]s.
